title: Conservation drift: does it preserve the invariant?
summary: Many physical systems have a quantity that should stay constant, such as energy. This plot shows how far each method's value strays, on a log axis, with the machine-epsilon floor drawn as a reference.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of energy error against time for four integrators: explicit Euler grows to about 1e4, symplectic Euler stays near 1e-2, Stormer-Verlet near 5e-4, RK4 creeps up to about 5e-7; a dotted machine-epsilon line at the bottom.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Does it preserve the invariant?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time t (0 to 200), linear. y: |E - E0|, the running maximum of the energy error, logarithmic from 1e-18 to 1e8.
look_at: Which curve grows without bound and which stay bounded?
At what level does each bounded curve sit, and is it flat or creeping upward?
How far is the best curve from the machine-epsilon line? A curve at the line cannot be improved.
Is the quantity plotted the running maximum or the instantaneous value? (A running maximum hides oscillation.)
as_drawn: Four methods on a harmonic oscillator with h = 0.05: explicit Euler (rose, solid), symplectic Euler (blue, dashed), RK4 (amber, dash-dot), Stormer-Verlet (teal, dotted).
Explicit Euler rises steadily to about 1e4 at t = 200. Symplectic Euler is flat at about 1e-2 and Stormer-Verlet flat at about 5e-4. RK4 starts near 1e-9 and creeps up to about 5e-7.
The machine-epsilon line sits at 2.2e-16, far below every curve; the y axis runs to 1e-18 so it is visible.
The y axis label says running max, so oscillations of the energy are hidden behind an envelope.
read_the_figure.proves: A curve that stays flat over a long run shows that the method conserves the invariant up to a bounded error; a curve that climbs steadily shows secular drift. Neither is a statement about the accuracy of the trajectory itself.
if_wrong: A curve rising with time: the method has secular drift, so long runs will fail.
A curve at the epsilon floor: the invariant is conserved to round-off, usually because the quantity is a quadratic invariant and the method preserves it exactly, or because the run is too short.
A curve above the floor that is flat: a bounded energy error whose size scales with a power of h.
must_check: log axis: the curves differ by twelve orders of magnitude, so only a logarithmic axis shows them together.
machine-epsilon floor: it marks the best a double-precision run can do, so the reader knows how much room remains.

terms.meaning: A quantity that is exactly constant along the true solution, such as the energy of a frictionless oscillator.
The deviation of the numerical invariant from its initial value, as a function of time or step size.
A deviation that grows steadily, usually linearly or exponentially, with time.
A method that preserves the symplectic structure of Hamiltonian flow. It does not conserve energy exactly but keeps its error bounded over very long times.
The spacing of floating-point numbers near 1, about 2.2e-16 in double precision.

remember: Explicit Euler on an oscillator multiplies the energy by 1 + h^2 every step.
Symplectic Euler and Stormer-Verlet: bounded energy error of order h and h^2.
RK4 on an oscillator loses energy by about h^6 / 72 relative per step: tiny, but always in one direction.
Bounded and small beats very small and drifting for long runs.
Nothing can go below the epsilon floor.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is time and on y the size of the energy error on a log scale; four line styles and colours separate the methods so no distinction depends on colour alone. The dotted horizontal line is not data but the smallest error double precision can represent. The y value is a running maximum, so each curve is non-decreasing.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: In plain words, a good method for a conservative system should not slowly pump energy in or out. Plotting the energy error against time lets you tell at once a flat line (bounded) from a rising line (drift). The log axis is what lets a drift of a factor of 1e4 and a bounded error of 1e-3 appear in the same frame.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A running maximum hides the oscillation of the error and can only rise, so a method that is merely oscillating looks as if it is drifting a little at the start. RK4's tiny drift looks excellent over 200 time units but would exceed Stormer-Verlet's bounded error after about 1e5 time units, a horizon the figure does not show. And energy conservation says nothing about phase error: a method can conserve energy and still put the planet in the wrong place.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the relative error |E - E0| / |E0| if E0 is not of order 1. Use a separate panel for phase error or for the trajectory difference. For long runs, plot against the number of steps and against the step size at a fixed final time to see the order of the bounded error.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Plot the instantaneous energy error as a faint band under the running maximum, add the same plot against step size h at a fixed final time, and mark the time at which RK4's drift crosses the symplectic curves.

steps.title: Explicit Euler pumps energy in
steps.note: The matrix has determinant 1 + h^2, so each step multiplies q^2 + p^2 by 1 + h^2.

steps.title: The drift over a run
steps.note: For h = 0.05 and T = 200 this gives e^10, a growth by a factor of about 2.2e4.

steps.title: RK4 loses a little each step
steps.note: The stability polynomial evaluated on the imaginary axis; verified symbolically. So RK4 damps the oscillator by a relative h^6/72 per step.

worked.title: Reading the conservation drift from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is explicit Euler's energy error at t = 200, and does the growth rate match 1 + h^2 per step? (2) At what level is symplectic Euler bounded, and is that consistent with an error of order h? (3) Extrapolating RK4's creep linearly, when would it cross Stormer-Verlet's flat level of about 3e-4?

solution.text: (1) The rose curve ends at about 1e4. Compute the prediction with h = 0.05 and 4000 steps.
That agrees with the plot, and the growth rate per time unit is ln(1 + h^2) / h, about 0.050, so an e-folding time of about 20.
(2) Symplectic Euler's bound is of order h; here h/4 = 0.0125.
(3) RK4 loses E0 h^6 / 72 per step, so the error after n steps is n times that.
That is about 2.8 million steps, or time 1.4e5, far beyond the plotted 200.

worked.answer: Explicit Euler is at about 1e4, matching (1 + h^2)^N; symplectic Euler is bounded near 1e-2, of order h. RK4's drift would cross the Stormer-Verlet level only after about 1.4e5 time units, so for short runs RK4 wins and for very long runs the symplectic method does.

analyze.q: Why does Stormer-Verlet sit about two orders of magnitude below symplectic Euler?
analyze.hint: Compare h to h^2 for h = 0.05.

analyze.q: Why is RK4's curve higher at the start than the epsilon line yet still rising slowly?
analyze.hint: Truncation error per step versus the number of steps.

analyze.q: The plot shows a running maximum. What would the instantaneous energy error of Stormer-Verlet look like?

evaluate.q: You need a ten-thousand-period orbit. Do you choose by this plot alone?
evaluate.hint: Phase error, cost per step, order of the bounded error.

create: Redraw the plot against the number of periods and add a vertical dashed line at the end of the run you plan to use.
Add a panel of the instantaneous energy error for the two symplectic methods so the oscillation is visible.

checks.q: Why does explicit Euler gain energy on an oscillator?
checks.hint: Look at the determinant of the one-step matrix.
checks.answer: The one-step matrix has determinant 1 + h^2 > 1, so q^2 + p^2 is multiplied by 1 + h^2 each step.

checks.q: h = 0.1 and 100 steps of explicit Euler. By what factor does the energy grow?
checks.answer: 1.01^100 = 2.70, so the energy grows by a factor of about 2.7 (that is, e^{hT} with T = 10).

checks.q: A method has an energy error that is flat at 1e-3 but its orbit drifts in phase. Is the plot wrong?
checks.answer: No: the plot measures only energy. A symplectic method can conserve energy bounded and still have a phase error that grows linearly; you need a trajectory-error plot as well.
